cards.title: Prioritize router and network-device exposure in the store environment
cards.summary: Routers, switches, and access points were the most commonly vulnerable class in the source's cited survey, and their compromise enables traffic interception or proxying for the whole store.
cards.use_when: Planning network security for a store or warehouse, or deciding what to harden first when local devices are in scope.

cards.title: Monitor inbound reachability and device updateability on the store local network
cards.summary: Most local devices assume that anything reaching them is trusted and rarely receive updates, so the firewall is often the only working control; verify what it actually blocks.
cards.use_when: Reviewing store or warehouse network policy, onboarding new IoT hardware (printers, cameras, displays), or responding to a suspected local-device compromise.

cards.title: DNS Rebinding: How an Attacker Turns a Visitor's Browser into a Proxy for Your Local Services
cards.summary: Explains the DNS rebinding mechanism so operators can recognize which local services and device integrations on their own network are exposed to browser-originated requests.
cards.use_when: Auditing store hardware, local sync utilities, label printers, or any locally-hosted admin service that your ecommerce staff run on machines also used for web browsing.

cards.title: Host Header Validation: The Standard Server-Side Defense Against DNS Rebinding
cards.summary: A local or device server should reject any request whose Host header is not its own expected hostname, enforced in middleware that runs before every route handler.
cards.use_when: Hardening any locally running service, device API, or integration helper that your store operates and that is reachable from a browser on the same machine or network.

cards.title: Host vs Origin Headers: Keeping the Two Checks Straight in Store Integrations
cards.summary: Origin identifies the page that initiated a request while Host identifies the destination the browser thinks it is reaching, and conflating them leaves rebinding defenses ineffective.
cards.use_when: Reviewing the request-validation code of an ecommerce integration, local print/sync agent, or any service that exposes an HTTP API to browsers.

cards.title: Reduce the Local-Server Attack Surface Before Adding Detection
cards.summary: Every avoidable local HTTP server is an unauthenticated API on the customer's or employee's machine, so the first control is architectural elimination.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing desktop companion apps, in-store device software, POS helpers, or any product that spins up a listener on the operator's machine.

cards.title: Rebinding Against Remote HTTPS Sites Is Largely Blunted by TLS and Cookies
cards.summary: A DNS flip toward a public site fails at the TLS certificate check and carries the wrong cookies, so rebinding's real power is confined to services that trust network position.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing which of your assets need rebinding protection: ranking local unauthenticated services above public HTTPS storefront endpoints.

cards.title: Resolver-Level Mitigation: Refusing DNS Answers That Point to Loopback or Private Ranges
cards.summary: A DNS resolver under your control can refuse answers that resolve to loopback or RFC1918 addresses, which neutralizes rebinding for everything behind it.
cards.use_when: Configuring network policy for a store's office, warehouse or back-of-house networks where unpatched devices live alongside browsing machines.

cards.title: Caching and Keep-Alive Timing Determine Whether Rebinding Succeeds at All
cards.summary: The attack depends on the victim's DNS cache expiring and the browser opening a fresh connection, which is why it is unreliable and repeated on a timer.
cards.use_when: Assessing residual risk from rebinding for a device or integration and deciding how confidently to claim a fix works.

cards.title: Real DNS Rebinding Incidents Show the Blast Radius: Update Agents and Background Daemons
cards.summary: Documented rebinding cases involved update agents and peer-to-peer client services that accepted unauthenticated commands, illustrating why any local listener is a liability.
cards.use_when: Assessing your own desktop software, updater, or background service for the same class of flaw before shipping or renewing a security review.

cards.title: Mirai as an Ecommerce-IoT Cautionary Case: Default Credentials and Internet-Facing Device Ports
cards.summary: A large-scale botnet built from consumer IoT devices exploited devices that listened on the open internet and shipped with default passwords, not a clever rebinding trick.
cards.use_when: Procuring any internet-connected device for a store — cameras, signage players, smart plugs, routers, thermostats — or drafting requirements for connected-device purchases.

cards.title: Bound Session Reuse of Local Admin Tools in Store Operations
cards.summary: Web-connected devices and local admin utilities should never be reachable from a browsing session that also touches external sites.
cards.use_when: Setting up in-store workstations, POS terminals, or back-office machines that use both web admin panels and general web browsing.

cards.title: Browser Engine Bugs Let Merely Visiting a Page Compromise the Machine
cards.summary: JavaScript engine flaws have allowed a plain web page to read and write arbitrary process memory, which is why a store workstation's browsing habits are a security control.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much general web browsing to permit on machines that handle customer data or payment-adjacent operations.

cards.title: Assume Breach at the Browser Layer and Design Store Systems for Containment
cards.summary: Because a browser compromise can read memory and issue commands, design store systems so a single compromised workstation or session cannot reach the whole operation.
cards.use_when: Architecting access for ecommerce back office, order management and payment tooling where staff use web browsers all day.

cards.title: Run a Bounded Rebinding Test Against Your Own Local Service
cards.summary: A controlled test confirms whether a local store service rejects hostname mismatches, and it must check the negative case with the socket, not just the response headers.
cards.use_when: Validating a fix to an updater, device API, or local companion service before shipping it or closing out a security finding.

cards.title: Enforce the Host Check at the Very Top of the Request Pipeline
cards.summary: Placing a security check inside a later, conditional function lets requests slip past it; the source's bug was fixed only by moving the check to the first code that runs.
cards.use_when: Implementing or reviewing request-validation middleware for any store service, integration endpoint or local device API.

cards.title: Decide How Much Local-Server Functionality Your Product Actually Needs
cards.summary: Legitimate use cases for a local server do exist, but each one must be weighed against a class of vulnerability that developers routinely get wrong.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing which local-service features to keep, redesign, or retire in store software and companion apps.

cards.title: Renderer/browser process separation to limit storefront breach damage
cards.summary: Isolate untrusted parsing (HTML, CSS, JS, images) in sandboxed renderer processes that must request file and network access through a privileged browser process, so a store takeover stays contained.
cards.use_when: Architecting or reviewing the security boundaries of a custom storefront, headless-rendering service, or in-house checkout so a rendering bug cannot touch customer data or admin files.

cards.title: Defend against memory-safety bugs as the dominant vulnerability class
cards.summary: Memory-corruption bugs make up most critical browser vulns, so choose memory-safe languages and isolation for code handling untrusted storefront input.
cards.use_when: Selecting a stack or writing parsers/decoders for untrusted store inputs (images, feeds, uploads, custom widgets) on a storefront or checkout service.

cards.title: Enforce strong auto-update for storefront dependencies
cards.summary: Ship automatic, non-optional updates for browser/agent components and dependencies so known vulns are closed without relying on users or admins.
cards.use_when: Designing update policy for a storefront, an in-store kiosk browser, an embedded widget, or a dependency pipeline.

cards.title: Use browser isolation and separate sessions for ecommerce administration
cards.summary: Apply browser containment principles to operational tools rather than attempting to implement the browser engine in store code.
cards.use_when: Running multi-tenant embeddable storefronts, marketplaces, or iframe-based checkout widgets where one origin could attack another.

cards.title: Harden JavaScript for storefront and checkout code
cards.summary: Use strict mode and a linter to eliminate coercive equality, duplicate keys, and prototype-pollution bugs that can crash order-processing servers.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing checkout, cart, pricing, or order-API JavaScript that handles user-submitted JSON and query data.

cards.title: Defend against automatic semicolon insertion pitfalls in storefront scripts
cards.summary: Unhandled ASI edge cases can silently change behavior or leave dead code, so run a linter regardless of whether you write semicolons.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing storefront, cart, or analytics JavaScript that mixes lines without semicolons or returns objects from functions.

cards.title: Prefer explicit, boring code over clever code in security-relevant paths
cards.summary: Overly clever JS (short-circuit tricks, spread-into-object one-liners, prototype calls) hides intent and hides bugs, so write explicit code for checkout, auth, and order logic.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or writing checkout, pricing, authentication, or order-processing code where readability and auditability matter more than brevity.

cards.title: Protect against the open-source and extension supply chain
cards.summary: A typical NPM install pulls in ~1,000+ packages from thousands of unvetted contributors; treat the dependency tree and browser extensions as an untrusted supply chain with real failure modes.
cards.use_when: Choosing dependencies for a storefront platform, adding a browser extension to your workflow, or assessing third-party scripts and widgets on product pages.

cards.title: Recognize targeted dependency attacks and account-takeover risk
cards.summary: Maintainer burnout and account takeover have produced targeted malware (e.g. an event-stream-style case), so pin, audit, and monitor dependencies rather than trusting reputation.
cards.use_when: Evaluating package maintainer activity, structuring a dependency policy, or investigating a suspicious release in your build pipeline.

cards.title: Apply defense-in-depth and a paranoid mindset to storefront security
cards.summary: Assume each control will fail and layer redundancy (sanitize input, hash passwords with bcrypt, use SameSite cookies) rather than trusting one measure.
cards.use_when: Designing overall security posture for a store account, checkout, admin panel, or integration layer.

cards.title: Write tests because untested code is broken code
cards.summary: The source asserts untested code is broken code, so add tests to checkout, pricing, cart, and order flows before trusting them in production.
cards.use_when: Shipping any storefront feature where a silent bug would cost revenue — pricing, discounts, tax, cart totals, order submission.

cards.title: Store passwords with a maintained adaptive password hasher
cards.summary: Use purpose-built password hashing with unique salts and tested cost settings rather than raw fast hashes or reversible encryption.
cards.use_when: Reviewing how your store platform, custom app or admin panel stores customer and staff login credentials.

cards.title: Ambient Authority via Cookies: Use SameSite
cards.summary: Browsers automatically attach cookies to requests for a site, which lets other origins trigger authenticated actions; SameSite cookies are the source's fix.
cards.use_when: Hardening cookie-based sessions for your storefront, customer accounts or admin panel so other sites cannot silently trigger authenticated requests.

cards.title: Prefer Explicit Code Over Clever Code in Store Systems
cards.summary: In security-relevant store code, choose boring, plain, repetitive and explicit implementations over magical abstractions.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or writing code that touches checkout, payments, authentication, refunds or customer data on your store.

cards.title: Make Dangerous Code Look Dangerous
cards.summary: Risky functions should have alarming names, clear documentation and should not be mixed with benign-looking operations.
cards.use_when: Naming and organizing internal APIs in your store platform — especially functions that move money, expose customer data or change account state.

cards.title: Adopt a Paranoid, Vigilant Security Mindset
cards.summary: The source treats constant paranoia and vigilance as a genuine asset when maintaining store security.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations and habits for whoever maintains your store's security posture over time — platform owner, in-house dev or agency.

cards.title: Smaller Packages Have Enlarged Modern Dependency Trees
cards.summary: Modern package managers enable many small packages with conflicting versions installed locally, so dependency trees and ecosystems are far larger than in older ecosystems.
cards.use_when: Assessing supply-chain and update risk for the libraries your storefront, checkout or integrations depend on.

cards.title: Standardized Collaboration Platforms Accelerated Code Flow
cards.summary: GitHub-style standardization means code moves faster and between more hands than in the older, per-project mailing-list era, expanding the trust surface.
cards.use_when: Evaluating the risk of third-party code, templates, plugins or themes you pull into your store from public repositories.

cards.title: AOV threshold gating with a hero SKU
cards.summary: Pull a disproportionately high-selling SKU from direct sale and gate it as a free gift above an AOV threshold to force larger carts.
cards.use_when: Designing an offer or merchandising plan to lift average order value when one product dominates sales.

cards.title: Use revenue and contribution per visitor to assess acquisition headroom
cards.summary: Combine purchase conversion, AOV and contribution with traffic cost before scaling.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to increase paid acquisition spend on a store, or diagnosing why scaling ad spend turns unprofitable.

cards.title: Lifetime gross profit vs Day-1 acquisition cost
cards.summary: Model 12-month Lifetime Gross Profit against Day-1 CAC to justify front-end losses on first purchase.
cards.use_when: Setting allowable CAC and deciding whether to accept a loss on a customer's first order to fund paid acquisition.

cards.title: Angle test before rebuilding the landing page
cards.summary: Test multiple ad angles against one generic page, then rewrite the whole page to match the winning angle.
cards.use_when: Improving paid social performance and deciding what messaging/creative should drive the product landing page.

cards.title: AI-assisted competitor ad scraping and UGC generation
cards.summary: Automate competitor ad analysis and turn top performers into UGC-style creative variations via a bot workflow.
cards.use_when: Producing paid social creative at volume and needing competitor inspiration without a manual research grind each week.

cards.title: Evaluate identity-resolution data before using it for ecommerce outreach
cards.summary: Assess the origin, permitted use and quality of matched visitor data before considering it for a marketing audience.
cards.use_when: Growing an email list from cold site traffic where many visitors bounce without signing up.

cards.title: Incentivized surveys to direct product expansion
cards.summary: Use everyone-wins survey incentives to extract open-ended objections and product requests from buyers.
cards.use_when: Deciding what products to add or how to position an existing catalog based on customer demand.

cards.title: Daily habit-stacking onboarding for consumables
cards.summary: Send daily emails for the first 90 days to force product consumption until use becomes a permanent habit.
cards.use_when: Retaining customers on consumable products (supplements, skincare, treatments) where repeat use drives reorders.

cards.title: AI intake funnel for store automation requests
cards.summary: Centralize automation wishlists through a form, bi-weekly prioritization, and a tracked assignee.
cards.use_when: Scaling ecommerce operations and needing a disciplined way to select which internal automations to build.

cards.title: Frame SOPs as the promotion prerequisite
cards.summary: Secure employee SOP compliance by tying documentation to promotion and pay, not to nagging.
cards.use_when: Getting store/ops staff to document their own processes so the company can scale and hire beneath them.

cards.title: Structure by pods and P&L for scaling operations
cards.summary: Organize teams into P&L-driven pods, districts, and departments for accountability.
cards.use_when: Reorganizing an ecommerce brand or agency operation as headcount grows and ownership blurs.

cards.title: Narrow ecommerce positioning around a specific product-use problem
cards.summary: Test whether a more specific use case makes the product's value clearer without assuming demographic targeting creates pricing power.
cards.use_when: Positioning a product and setting price, when a broad audience description isn't converting or sustaining premium pricing.

cards.title: Calculate Lifetime Gross Profit, Not Day-One Profit, to Set Your CAC Ceiling
cards.summary: Judge customer profitability over 12 months of gross profit, not first-purchase margin, when deciding how much you can spend to acquire a customer.
cards.use_when: Pricing decisions and acquisition budget setting — when you are deciding the maximum acceptable CAC for a product or evaluating whether to keep scaling paid traffic on a low-margin first purchase.

cards.title: Use Conversion Rate × AOV ≈ 300 as a Scalability Screen
cards.summary: A revenue-per-100-visitors check (conversion rate % × AOV) of roughly 300 is the source's threshold for whether paid traffic can profitably scale.
cards.use_when: Acquisition and pricing decisions — when auditing whether a store can sustain paid traffic at scale, or deciding whether to take on / continue ad spend for a brand.

cards.title: Turn a Coveted Hero SKU Into a Spend-Threshold Gift to Raise AOV
cards.summary: Find the product customers already want most, stop selling it outright, and give it free only above a spend threshold to lift AOV.
cards.use_when: Merchandising and AOV decisions — when you have a hero SKU with outsized demand and want to raise average order value without discounting core products.

cards.title: Test Angles at the Ad Level Before Touching the Landing Page
cards.summary: Run multiple creative angles quickly, read CTR to find the winner, then rebuild the PDP/landing page to match that angle.
cards.use_when: Landing page and acquisition creative decisions — when a product's messaging isn't landing and you need a fast, cheap way to find the angle before investing in page redesign.

cards.title: Pivot Only After Genuine Effort and Multi-Demographic Testing Fail
cards.summary: Treat persistent friction selling as a product-market-fit or wrong-audience signal, but only after broad, real testing — not premature quitting.
cards.use_when: Product selection and positioning decisions — when deciding whether to pivot a struggling store's product or audience.

cards.title: Model Repeat Purchases Around Consumption Rate, Not Stockpile Offers
cards.summary: Large bulk offers can hurt repeat purchase if customers stop using the product; size offers so they're actually consumed and stay on subscription.
cards.use_when: Bundles and replenishment/subscription design — when deciding offer size (single vs multi-unit) and how to keep customers re-buying in consumable categories like supplements.

cards.title: Use Email/SMS Surveys With Incentives to Mine Objections and Adjacent Products
cards.summary: Reward customers (and non-buyers) with a giveaway plus store credit to collect open-ended answers that reveal buy reasons, objections and product ideas.
cards.use_when: Customer research and product roadmap decisions — when you need to learn why people buy or don't, or what to launch next.

cards.title: Require a Front-End Welcome/Abandoned Flow Before Scaling Paid Traffic
cards.summary: Treat a solid email/SMS welcome and abandoned-cart system as a precondition to profitable scaling — the source estimates ~15% acquisition lift.
cards.use_when: Retention and acquisition decisions — when preparing to scale paid traffic and deciding whether your email/SMS foundation is ready.

cards.title: Structure Teams as Profit-Owning Pods Under Districts and Departments
cards.summary: Organize pods of teams into districts under department heads, each led by a strategist who owns the P&L and shares in team profit.
cards.use_when: Team and operations decisions — when structuring an agency or in-house ecommerce operation by channel and holding people accountable to profit.

cards.title: Run a Company-Wide Automation Intake Funnel for AI Developer Priorities
cards.summary: Collect automation requests via a simple form, prioritize them bi-weekly by company impact, and assign an AI developer to build the highest-value ones.
cards.use_when: Operations and internal automation decisions — when deciding what to build first with a dedicated AI/dev resource and avoiding scattered, role-specific side projects.

cards.title: Feed a Single Per-Client Profile So AI Can Summarize Accounts
cards.summary: Centralize all notes, tasks and updates for each client into one profile so an AI tool can pull and summarize account status across clients.
cards.use_when: Operations and account management decisions — when you need fast cross-account visibility and want AI to answer questions about many clients at once.

cards.title: Hire a Dedicated Internal AI Developer, Not Just Scattered Tinkerers
cards.summary: The source argues every company needs a dedicated AI developer; he sources one offshore at ~$3.5k/month to build company-priority automations.
cards.use_when: Operations and hiring decisions — when deciding whether and how to staff internal automation and AI builder capacity.

cards.title: Secure SOP Compliance by Framing Documentation as the Promotion Gate
cards.summary: Get 100% of employees to write their own replacement SOPs by making documentation the stated prerequisite for promotion.
cards.use_when: Operations and team-scaling decisions — when you need reliable process documentation so you can hire beneath people and scale without the founder bottlenecking.

cards.title: Shift the CAC Question From 'Lower It' to 'Make It Work'
cards.summary: Rather than grinding to cut CAC from ~$70 to ~$60, improve retention and lifetime gross profit so your current CAC becomes profitable.
cards.use_when: Acquisition and pricing decisions — when paid traffic is near break-even and cutting CAC further feels hard or not worth the effort.

cards.title: Prefer Influencer/Affiliate Virality on TikTok Over Paid-Only Traffic
cards.summary: The source names TikTok creator-economy virality (commission-only influencer posts) as the largest current traffic arbitrage opportunity.
cards.use_when: Acquisition channel decisions — when evaluating where to allocate attention and paid budget across channels.

cards.title: Centralize AI/automation requests in one intake form and prioritize them on a shared board
cards.summary: Collect internal automation and AI requests through one form, filter them in a recurring leadership review, and only push the approved ones onto a single prioritized project board with time estimates.
cards.use_when: You want to systematize internal automation and tooling work for an ecommerce operation (product data sync, inventory alerts, ad reporting, customer-service macros) instead of letting requests ping-pong across the team.

cards.title: Get manager buy-in before rolling out any cross-store initiative
cards.summary: Before pushing a new company-wide process, validate it with the managers who will run it and reframe the 'why' in terms of what's in it for the person doing the work.
cards.use_when: You are about to standardize a recurring ecommerce task across many stores or clients — a new weekly reporting ritual, a PDP refresh checklist, a review-request process — and need it to actually get done without you checking every instance.

cards.title: Handle entrepreneurial hires with a clear verbal commitment and a clean exit norm
cards.summary: The source deliberately hires entrepreneurial people for roles like media buying and dev/automation, asks for a spoken minimum commitment, and keeps exits clean and relationship-preserving.
cards.use_when: You're hiring for a growth-critical ecommerce role (paid media, retention/CRM, CRO/dev, creative production) and are weighing a strong candidate who openly plans to build their own business.

cards.title: Ask 'can I hand this off?' before 'should I handle this?'
cards.summary: Make delegation the default first question so your own time is reserved for the few high-leverage plays only you can execute, with a personal idea-capture list so big swings don't get buried.
cards.use_when: You're the operator of an ecommerce brand and your day is full of requests, fires and small tasks while ad campaigns, partnerships and bigger merchandising plays keep getting postponed.

cards.title: Break the 'bigger box' trap before scaling past a plateau
cards.summary: The source warns that growing revenue by piling tasks onto the same founder-built machine just enlarges the box you're trapped in, so periodically rebuild the foundation instead.
cards.use_when: Your ecommerce brand has reached a revenue plateau (the source names around $100k/month as a reflection point) and your own hours are scaling up with revenue instead of staying flat.

cards.title: Build the founder's personal brand as a distribution asset, not a vanity project
cards.summary: The source's top takeaway from a founder event: the operators with the most inbound opportunities all had large personal brands, so start publishing earlier rather than later.
cards.use_when: You run an ecommerce brand and want a durable channel for partnerships, creator collabs, retail/distribution deals or inbound talent that doesn't depend on paid acquisition.

cards.title: Separate New vs Existing Customer Ad Spend
cards.summary: Segment paid media reporting by new and returning customers so you can see whether spend is buying growth or just harvesting people who would buy anyway.
cards.use_when: Auditing or restructuring paid acquisition for your store when topline revenue has plateaued despite a reported 'healthy' ROAS.

cards.title: Why ROAS Is a Flawed Primary KPI
cards.summary: ROAS fails as a north-star metric because it is last-click, easily skewed by existing customers, and drives budget misallocation toward bottom-of-funnel.
cards.use_when: Choosing which marketing KPI to report to leadership or to optimize daily spend against for your store.

cards.title: Split Klaviyo Attributed Revenue by New vs Returning
cards.summary: Klaviyo-attributed revenue is a useful north-star but is inflated by default view-through-style settings and should be split by customer type.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing your email/SMS retention KPIs and deciding whether to optimize campaigns for attributed revenue.

cards.title: Frequency Audit as a First Step to Cutting Existing-Customer Waste
cards.summary: A simple frequency check in the ad account reveals how heavily you are re-targeting buyers and gives an intuitive basis for pulling budget.
cards.use_when: Preparing an audit or budget-review of your store's paid media, especially existing-customer targeting.

cards.title: Match Ad Spend Allocation to Your Repurchase Cycle
cards.summary: How much to spend re-targeting existing customers depends on how often your product can realistically be repurchased.
cards.use_when: Deciding budget split between acquisition and existing/retention-oriented paid media for your specific product category.

cards.title: Treat Awareness-Funnel Spend Cautiously but Recognize It Drives Sales
cards.summary: Top-of-funnel activity can be genuinely valuable yet unmeasurable in last-click systems, so it gets under-funded relative to retargeting.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget across the funnel and interpreting reports that show strong branded/retargeting ROAS versus weak upper-funnel numbers.

cards.title: Measure Retention by Fundamentals, Not Email KPIs
cards.summary: Retention is primarily driven by product, portfolio, customer experience and pricing; email and owned media amplify, they rarely fix, weak retention.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing poor repeat purchase rates before investing in more email flows, upsells or cross-sells.

cards.title: Tie Spend Scaling to Net Profit, Not Absolute Budget
cards.summary: Scaling is not the same as increasing spend; the source reframes the goal as profitable growth rather than revenue at any cost.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to raise ad budgets, or evaluating advice that tells you to simply spend more on Meta.

cards.title: Score Metrics by Whether They Hold Up in Any Context
cards.summary: A practical filter for choosing KPIs: prefer metrics that remain meaningful no matter the business model, time frame or channel.
cards.use_when: Selecting which metrics to hold as your north star and which to demote to context-only when managing your store's performance.

cards.title: Debug a Reported ROAS That Doesn't Match Topline
cards.summary: When reported ROAS stays healthy but revenue is flat, the likely cause is that spend is harvesting existing or high-intent buyers rather than acquiring new ones.
cards.use_when: Investigating a store where the ad account reports a 'healthy' ROAS (e.g. 4-5x) but total revenue has plateaued for months.

cards.title: Contrast as the Core Marketing Principle
cards.summary: Make every ad, email and store asset stand out from the noise by doing the opposite of what the market already sees.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative or email subject lines and unsure whether the idea will get noticed in a crowded feed or inbox.

cards.title: Purple Ocean: Carve a Segment Inside a Proven Market
cards.summary: Enter a market with proven demand, then narrow to a hyperspecific segment you can own 100% instead of fighting for a slice of a red ocean.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product or angle to launch, or repositioning an existing store into a defensible niche.
